chunks: "The main trade-off is efficiency versus simplicity and noise.
An LDO is just a pass transistor, so its efficiency is about V out over V in and all the difference is burned as heat. From 12 volts to 3. 3 volts at 1 amps that's 8.
7 watts, which won't work, while a buck would be about 90% and lose under a watt. So at large headroom or high current, the buck wins and the LDO is out.
But the LDO wins on everything else. It has no switching, so no inductor, no ripple, and no EMI.
It's quiet, it has high power-supply rejection at low frequency, and it has a fast response to load steps. It needs only a couple of capacitors, so it's tiny and cheap.
It has very low quiescent current options for battery standby. And it works when the input is close to the output.
The usual way I'd resolve it: if headroom is small, or the load is tiny, or the rail feeds sensitive analog or RF, use an LDO.
If headroom is big and the current is more than a few hundred milliamps, use a buck. And when you need both, buck down to just above the target, then an LDO to clean it up.
A charge pump sits in between: no inductor, but fixed ratios and limited current."
